n: In Iconium, Paul and Barnabas again began in the synagogue, and they taught so powerfully that many Jews and Greeks believed.

f.g: Modern Konya, in central Turkey.

n: Jewish leaders who rejected the message turned the Gentile population against the missionaries, poisoning their minds.

f.g: Embittered, hostile.

n: Still, they stayed a long time and spoke boldly. The Lord confirmed their message about his grace with miracles.
The city split into two camps — some sided with the Jewish opponents, others with the apostles. Luke calls Barnabas and Paul “apostles,” meaning ones sent forth.

f.g: Greek apostoloi — “those sent.” Here used in its broad sense of commissioned messengers.

n: A plot formed among Gentiles, Jews, and local leaders to mistreat and stone the missionaries.

f.g: Shamefully, with insult.

n: Learning of the plan, they fled to Lystra and Derbe, towns in the region of Lycaonia. Wise retreat let the work continue elsewhere.

f.g: Aware.
A Roman colony; later the hometown of Timothy (Acts 16:1).

n: Wherever they went, even as refugees, they kept preaching.
At Lystra was a man who had been lame from birth and had never walked. Luke, a physician, describes his condition three ways to show how hopeless it was.

f.g: Powerless, without strength.

n: As the man listened, Paul looked intently at him and saw that he had faith to be healed. Faith came through hearing the word.

f.w: he had faith to be healed

n: Paul commanded him to stand, and the man leaped up and walked. The healing echoes Peter’s miracle at the temple gate.
The crowd, speaking their native Lycaonian language, concluded the gods had come to earth in human form. A local legend told of Zeus and Hermes visiting this region in disguise.

f.w: The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men
f.g: Ovid’s Metamorphoses tells of Zeus and Hermes visiting nearby Phrygia in disguise.

n: They called Barnabas “Jupiter” (Zeus, king of the gods) and Paul “Mercurius” (Hermes, the messenger god), since Paul did the talking.

f.g: Roman name for Zeus, chief Greek god.
Mercury — Roman name for Hermes, the gods’ spokesman.

n: The priest of Zeus, whose temple stood outside the city, brought oxen decorated with wreaths to offer sacrifices to them.

f.g: Wreaths of wool or flowers placed on sacrificial animals.

n: When Barnabas and Paul realized what was happening, they tore their clothes — a sign of horror at blasphemy — and rushed into the crowd.

f.g: Tore their garments, a Jewish expression of grief or outrage at blasphemy.

n: “We’re only human, just like you!” they cried. Their message was to turn away from empty idols to the living God, Creator of everything.

f.w: men of like passions with you
f.g: People with the same nature and feelings as you.
Empty, worthless things — here, idols.

f.w: which made heaven, and earth, and the sea

n: In past ages God allowed the nations to go their own way, without the fuller revelation given to Israel.

f.g: Allowed, permitted.

n: Even so, God left evidence of himself in his kindness — rain, harvests, food, and joy. Paul begins with what pagans already know: nature itself testifies of God.

f.w: he left not himself without witness

n: Even with these words, they could barely stop the crowd from sacrificing to them.

f.g: Scarcely, barely.

n: Opponents from Antioch and Iconium followed them, turned the crowd, and stoned Paul. They dragged him out of the city thinking he was dead. The fickle crowd moved from worship to violence.
As disciples gathered around him, Paul got up and walked back into the city. The next day he left for Derbe — a remarkable recovery.

f.g: A town about 60 miles southeast of Lystra.

n: After making many disciples in Derbe, they bravely retraced their route through the very cities that had persecuted them.
They strengthened the new converts and warned them that entering God’s kingdom involves trials. Faith was not promised to be easy.

f.g: Strengthening, establishing.

n: They ordained elders to lead each branch and, with prayer and fasting, entrusted them to the Lord. The Church was organized with local priesthood leadership.

f.g: Greek cheirotoneō — appointed, literally “stretched out the hand.”

n: They passed back through the Pisidia region and came down to the coastal area of Pamphylia.
They preached in Perga, which they had skipped earlier, and then went to the port of Attalia.

f.g: Modern Antalya, a port on Turkey’s southern coast.

n: From there they sailed back to Antioch in Syria, where their mission had begun. Their assignment was complete.

f.w: recommended to the grace of God

n: They gathered the church and reported everything God had done — especially how he opened “the door of faith” to the Gentiles.
Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch a long while with the believers, resting and teaching before the next challenge arose.
